topics.name: Recursion
topics.kicker: A function that calls itself · Breaks big problems into smaller copies
topics.briefing: Recursion is a programming trick in which a function solves a big problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem, like a set of Russian nesting dolls. Every recursive function needs a base case, a simple answer that stops the chain; forget it, and the calls can pile up until the program crashes with a “stack overflow.” Programmers use recursion to compute factorials, sort lists, and solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
topics.answerHtml: recursion (accept word forms like recursive functions; prompt on self-reference; do not accept “iteration” or “loops”)

tossups.p: Douglas Hofstadter’s book _Gödel, Escher, Bach_ explores this idea through art, music, and math. His joking “law” uses it by saying that a task always takes longer than you expect, “even when you take into account Hofstadter’s Law.”
tossups.r: In programming, this idea needs a base case to stop. For 10 points, name this technique in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Édouard Lucas [“ay-DWAR loo-KAH”] introduced a puzzle in 1883 under the anagram pen name “N. Claus de Siam.” Its shortest solution uses this technique: move all but the biggest disk out of the way, move the biggest disk, then move the smaller stack back on top.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used to solve the Tower of Hanoi, in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Wilhelm Ackermann published a function in 1928 that is defined using this idea and grows unbelievably fast. A program can use this idea to explore tree-shaped data, such as folders stored inside other folders on a computer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used to compute n factorial, in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Euclid’s method for the greatest common divisor can be written with this technique: the answer for a and b equals the answer for b and the remainder when a is divided by b, stopping when that remainder is 0. Merge sort and quicksort also use this technique to sort lists.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique in which a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it.

tossups.p: The name GNU is a joke version of this idea, because it stands for “GNU’s Not Unix,” so the name appears inside its own meaning. The name of the program WINE works the same way, since it stands for “Wine Is Not an Emulator.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this idea, which in programming describes a function that calls itself until it reaches a base case.

tossups.p: The Droste [“DROSS-tuh”] effect, named for a Dutch cocoa box showing a nurse carrying a cup of hot chocolate and a box with the same picture, is a visual example of this idea. Two mirrors facing each other create a similar picture inside a picture that seems to go on forever.
tossups.r: A program that uses it must reach a base case, or it may crash. For 10 points, name this idea, which in programming means a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Many compilers perform an optimization named for the “tail” of a function, which lets certain uses of this technique run without using up extra memory. Without that trick, each step of this technique adds another frame to the call stack.
tossups.r: If the calls never reach a base case, the program can crash with a stack overflow. For 10 points, name this technique in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Two of the first languages to allow this technique were John McCarthy’s Lisp, which relied heavily on it, and ALGOL 60. Each call made this way in a running program gets its own frame on the call stack.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique in which a function solves a problem by calling itself.

tossups.p: In the “mutual” form of this technique, two functions call each other back and forth, like an “is even” function and an “is odd” function. Any problem solved with this technique can also be solved using loops and a stack that the programmer manages.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used to solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: Without memoization [“MEM-oh-ih-ZAY-shun”], a trick that saves answers already found, a program that uses this technique can need billions of calls to find the 50th term of a famous sequence, because nearly every call makes two more.
tossups.r: That sequence is the Fibonacci sequence. For 10 points, name this technique in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: A proof by mathematical induction works much like this technique, proving a starting case and then showing that each case follows from the one before. Grammar uses a similar idea when a phrase holds a smaller phrase of the same kind, as in “the cat that chased the rat that ate the cheese.”
tossups.r: In programming, it needs a base case so it eventually stops. For 10 points, name this idea in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: John von Neumann described merge sort in 1945; it uses this technique to split a list in half, sort each half the same way, and then merge the two sorted halves. Binary search can also be written with this technique, checking the middle item and then searching only one half.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique in which a function calls itself on a smaller part of a problem.

tossups.p: Tony Hoare’s 1959 sorting method, quicksort, picks a “pivot” item, splits a list into smaller and larger items, and then sorts each part using this technique. Fractal shapes such as the Koch snowflake can be drawn the same way.
tossups.r: Every use of this technique needs a base case. For 10 points, name this technique in which a function calls itself.

tossups.p: The Sierpiński [“sher-PEEN-skee”] triangle is made by removing the middle of a triangle to leave three smaller triangles and then doing the same thing to each of those, a picture of this idea. A Logo program can use this idea to draw a tree in which every branch splits into two smaller trees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this idea, which programmers use when they write a function that calls itself on smaller inputs.

tossups.p: A popular question-and-answer website for programmers, founded in 2008, is named for an error that can happen when this technique goes too deep. As a joke, Google answered searches for this technique’s name by asking “Did you mean” the very same word.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used to compute factorials, in which a function calls itself.

Fibonacci numbers: each term is found by calling the same function on the two terms before it
Tower of Hanoi: move the smaller disks aside, move the biggest, then stack the smaller ones back on top; n disks take 2 to the n, minus 1 moves
Divide-and-conquer methods use it: merge sort sorts each half of a list the same way, and binary search checks the middle, then searches one half
Quicksort picks a pivot, splits a list into smaller and larger items, and sorts each part the same way
Anything done this way can also be done with loops (iteration) plus a stack the programmer manages
Used to explore tree-shaped data, such as folders stored inside other folders
Fractals such as the Koch snowflake and Sierpiński triangle are drawn by repeating one rule on smaller and smaller pieces
The Droste effect, a picture that contains itself, is named for a Dutch cocoa box; two facing mirrors make a similar endless picture
Édouard Lucas introduced the Tower of Hanoi puzzle in 1883 under the anagram pen name “N. Claus de Siam”
Hofstadter’s Law: a task always takes longer than you expect, “even when you take into account Hofstadter’s Law”; Douglas Hofstadter also wrote _Gödel, Escher, Bach_
Acronyms that contain themselves, like GNU (“GNU’s Not Unix”) and WINE (“Wine Is Not an Emulator”)
Wilhelm Ackermann’s function (1928), defined this way, grows unbelievably fast
Euclid’s algorithm: the greatest common divisor of a and b equals that of b and the remainder of a ÷ b, stopping when the remainder is 0
Memoization saves answers already found, so a slow Fibonacci program that makes billions of calls becomes fast
Tail-call optimization: when the self-call is a function’s last step, a compiler can turn it into a loop that uses no extra stack
In the mutual form, two functions call each other, like an “is even” function and an “is odd” function
John McCarthy’s Lisp (1958), which relied heavily on it, and ALGOL 60 were two of the first languages to allow it
John von Neumann described merge sort in 1945; Tony Hoare invented quicksort in 1959
Proof by mathematical induction works like it: prove a starting case, then show each case follows from the one before
Grammar uses it when a phrase holds a smaller phrase of the same kind, as in “the cat that chased the rat that ate the cheese”
The programmers’ question-and-answer website Stack Overflow (founded 2008) is named for the error it can cause
As a joke, Google answered searches for its name with “Did you mean” the very same word

trap.title: Self-call or loop?
trap.body: Recursion and iteration (loops) can solve the same problems, so a tossup about repeating steps may want either one. Other answer lines sit close by: the factorial function and the Fibonacci sequence are famous examples, “stack overflow” is the error recursion can cause, and a “recurrence relation” is a math rule that builds each term of a sequence from earlier terms.
trap.fix: Listen for “calls itself,” “defined in terms of itself,” or “base case”: that means recursion. “Repeats a block of code while a condition is true” or “for each item in a list” means a loop, or iteration. If every clue is about one example, like the pattern 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, answer that example instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: recursion (accept word forms like recursive functions; prompt on self-reference; do not accept “iteration” or “loops”)

topics.name: Alan Turing
topics.kicker: A founder of computer science · Helped crack Germany’s Enigma code
topics.briefing: Alan Turing was a British mathematician who imagined a simple machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape, an idea that became the basic model of what every computer can do. During World War II he worked at Bletchley Park, where machines he designed, called bombes, helped read Germany’s secret Enigma messages. He also asked whether machines could think, and computer science’s highest honor, the Turing Award, is named for him.
topics.answerHtml: Alan Turing (accept Turing; do not accept “Turing machine” or “Turing test”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1938 Princeton dissertation, supervised by Alonzo Church, this man introduced “oracle” machines that can answer questions no ordinary machine can. Two years earlier, he and Church had each shown that David Hilbert’s “decision problem” has no general solution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who imagined a computing machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape.

tossups.p: This man invented a statistical method named for Banbury, the town where its long paper sheets were printed, to help find the daily settings of German navy messages. He led Hut 8 and designed machines called bombes that built on earlier work by Polish codebreakers.
tossups.r: Those machines helped break the Enigma code. For 10 points, name this Bletchley Park codebreaker of World War II.

tossups.p: This man’s 1952 paper “The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis” [“mor-foh-JEN-uh-sis”] showed how chemicals that react and spread through tissue could form patterns like the spots and stripes on animals. Patterns of that kind are named for him.
tossups.r: Earlier, he imagined a machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape. For 10 points, name this British pioneer of computer science.

tossups.p: This man’s 1950 paper in the journal _Mind_ opens, “I propose to consider the question, ‘Can machines think?’” It predicted that by about the year 2000, an average judge would have no better than a 70 percent chance of spotting a computer after five minutes of questions.
tossups.r: That paper described the “imitation game,” a test later named for him. For 10 points, name this British computer scientist.

tossups.p: With David Champernowne [“CHAM-per-nown”], this man wrote an early chess program called Turochamp that no computer of the time could run. In 1952, he played a full game with it by working through its steps himself with pencil and paper.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician, the namesake of computer science’s top prize and of a test for machine intelligence.

tossups.p: At the National Physical Laboratory after World War II, this man designed the Automatic Computing Engine, or ACE, one of the first detailed plans for a computer that stores its programs in memory. He later wrote a programmers’ handbook for an early computer at the University of Manchester.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician, the namesake of a test of whether a machine can pass for a human.

tossups.p: The online puzzles called CAPTCHAs are named with an acronym that includes this man’s name, because they check whether a user is a human or a computer program. He suggested that instead of building an adult mind, scientists could build a “child machine” and teach it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British computer pioneer who proposed a test in which a judge types questions to try to tell a human from a machine.

tossups.p: In 1952, this man was convicted under British laws that then made relationships between men a crime. Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologized for his treatment in 2009, and Queen Elizabeth II granted him a royal pardon in 2013.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician and World War II codebreaker, whose portrait was put on the Bank of England’s £50 note in 2021.

tossups.p: In July 1942, this man worked out a hand method for finding the wheel patterns of the German Lorenz cipher, nicknamed “Tunny.” Later that year, he traveled to the United States to work with U.S. Navy codebreakers, and at Bell Labs he met Claude Shannon.
tossups.r: He also helped break the Enigma code. For 10 points, name this British codebreaker who worked at Bletchley Park during World War II.

tossups.p: Andrew Hodges wrote a 1983 biography of this man subtitled _The Enigma_. Derek Jacobi played this man in _Breaking the Code_, Hugh Whitemore’s 1986 play based on that book.
tossups.r: Hodges’s book also inspired the 2014 film _The Imitation Game_, starring Benedict Cumberbatch. For 10 points, name this British mathematician and Bletchley Park codebreaker.

tossups.p: This man proved a version of the central limit theorem in his King’s College, Cambridge, fellowship dissertation, not knowing that Jarl Lindeberg had already proved it in 1922. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1951.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who described a “universal” machine that could carry out any other machine’s instructions.

tossups.p: Conway’s Game of Life and the redstone circuits in _Minecraft_ are both “complete” in a sense named for this man, meaning that, given enough time and memory, they can carry out any computation a computer can.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British pioneer of computer science, whose imaginary machine reads and writes symbols on a tape.

tossups.p: David Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem [“ent-SHY-doongs-pro-BLAYM”] asked for a method that could decide whether any statement in logic is provable. In a 1936 paper, this man showed that no such method exists, and he proved that no general method can decide whether any given program will eventually stop.
tossups.r: That paper was “On Computable Numbers.” For 10 points, name this British mathematician, whose imaginary machines became the basic model of what computers can do.

tossups.p: This man was appointed an OBE in 1946 for wartime work that stayed secret for decades. In 2021, the Bank of England put his portrait on its new £50 note, which entered circulation on his birthday, June 23.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who helped break Germany’s Enigma code at Bletchley Park during World War II.

tossups.p: This man described a “universal” machine that could imitate any other machine of its kind just by reading a coded description of it, an early version of the idea of a computer that stores its own programs. He introduced these machines in the 1936 paper “On Computable Numbers.”
tossups.r: He also proposed a famous test of machine intelligence. For 10 points, name this British mathematician whose imaginary computing machines are named for him.

trap.title: The man, not his machine
trap.body: Many things are named for Alan Turing: the Turing machine, the Turing test, the Turing Award, and “Turing complete” systems. A tossup about the man may mention them as “named for this man,” and players who just heard about the machine blurt out “Turing machine,” which is wrong. Others mix him up with John von Neumann, whose 1945 report described the stored-program computer, or with Charles Babbage, who designed mechanical computers in the 1800s.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this man,” “this mathematician,” or “this codebreaker,” say just “Turing” or “Alan Turing.” Babbage clues mention the Difference Engine, the Analytical Engine, and Ada Lovelace; von Neumann clues mention the Manhattan Project and game theory. Colossus, the Bletchley Park computer used against the Lorenz cipher, was built by Tommy Flowers, not Turing.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alan Turing (accept Turing; do not accept “Turing machine” or “Turing test”)

topics.name: Java (programming language)
topics.kicker: Programming language from Sun Microsystems · Write once, run anywhere
topics.briefing: Java is a programming language that James Gosling’s team at Sun Microsystems released in 1995; it was first called Oak and then renamed after Java coffee. Its promise was “write once, run anywhere”: Java code is turned into bytecode that runs on a Java Virtual Machine, so the same program works on almost any device. It became a favorite for Android apps, school computer science classes, and the original version of _Minecraft_.
topics.answerHtml: Java (prompt on “Java Virtual Machine” or “JVM”; do not accept “JavaScript”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 2021, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6–2 that Google’s copying of code interfaces from this language for its phone software was fair use, ending a lawsuit that Oracle had filed in 2010. Justice Stephen Breyer wrote the court’s majority opinion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this programming language from Sun Microsystems, whose slogan was “write once, run anywhere.”

tossups.p: Mike Sheridan and Patrick Naughton helped start the 1991 “Green Project,” which created this language for consumer devices such as interactive TV boxes rather than for the web, where it later became popular. This language’s cartoon mascot is named Duke.
tossups.r: This language’s lead designer was James Gosling. For 10 points, name this language, named after a type of coffee.

tossups.p: Lambda expressions were added to this language in version 8, released in 2014. A program in this language traditionally starts at a method declared “public static void main,” and prints text with System.out.println [“print-LINE”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language, whose code is compiled into bytecode for a virtual machine named after it.

tossups.p: Scala, Clojure [“CLOH-zhur”], and Kotlin can all be compiled to the same bytecode as this language, so they run on its virtual machine. In 2019, Google said Kotlin was its preferred language for making Android apps.
tossups.r: Many Android apps had been written in this language before that. For 10 points, name this language created by James Gosling.

tossups.p: In 2006, this language’s makers began releasing it as free, open-source software called OpenJDK. Four years later, the database company Oracle bought those makers and took control of this language.
tossups.r: This language’s logo is a steaming cup of coffee. For 10 points, name this programming language released by Sun Microsystems in 1995.

tossups.p: This language was first named Oak, after a tree outside its lead designer’s office, but that name had to be changed because another company already owned it as a trademark.
tossups.r: Its new name came from a kind of coffee. For 10 points, name this language that James Gosling created at Sun Microsystems.

tossups.p: Small programs written in this language, called applets, once ran inside web browsers, until browsers stopped supporting them in the 2010s. This language’s compiler turns code into bytecode that runs on a virtual machine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language from Sun Microsystems that promised programmers they could “write once, run anywhere.”

tossups.p: This language has exactly eight “primitive” data types, including int, double, and boolean, while text is stored in objects of its String class. Its source code is compiled into bytecode for a virtual machine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language, created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems, whose slogan was “write once, run anywhere.”

tossups.p: Interactive menus on many Blu-ray discs run on a system based on this language, and a tiny version of it runs on the chips in many SIM cards and bank cards. Its compiled programs can run on any device that has its virtual machine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language created by James Gosling, whose slogan was “write once, run anywhere.”

tossups.p: Google built the Dalvik [“DAL-vik”] virtual machine, named for a fishing village in Iceland, as its own replacement for this language’s standard virtual machine, and it later replaced Dalvik with a system called ART.
tossups.r: Both ran Android apps, which were long written mostly in this language. For 10 points, name this language released by Sun Microsystems in 1995.

tossups.p: Brendan Eich wrote a scripting language for the Netscape browser in about ten days in 1995; although its name was chosen partly to ride on this language’s popularity, the two are completely different languages.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language from Sun Microsystems, whose name comes from a kind of coffee.

tossups.p: Every piece of code in this language must sit inside a class, because it was designed from the start around objects. Its curly-brace syntax was borrowed largely from C and C++.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this object-oriented language that Sun Microsystems released in 1995, whose logo is a coffee cup.

tossups.p: This language’s “garbage collector” automatically frees memory that a program no longer uses, so, unlike programmers in C, its programmers rarely manage memory by hand. Its compiler turns source files into bytecode.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this language whose mascot is Duke and whose logo is a cup of coffee.

tossups.p: Starting in the 2000s, the College Board’s AP Computer Science A exam tested students in this object-oriented language. Its standard library includes the ArrayList class, which appears on that exam.
tossups.r: Markus Persson wrote the first version of _Minecraft_ in this language. For 10 points, name this language created at Sun Microsystems.

tossups.p: Programmers in this language can build windows and buttons with toolkits named AWT and Swing, and they often package finished programs into JAR files. Its virtual machine checks each program’s bytecode for safety before running it.
tossups.r: The first version of _Minecraft_ was written in this language. For 10 points, name this language, released by Sun Microsystems in 1995.

trap.title: Java, not JavaScript!
trap.body: Java and JavaScript sound alike but are completely different languages. JavaScript was written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995 to make web pages interactive, and its name was chosen partly to ride on Java’s popularity. Players also hear “Java” and think of the Indonesian island or of coffee; the language was named after Java coffee, but the island is its own answer line.
trap.fix: Java clues: James Gosling, Sun Microsystems, Oak, bytecode and its virtual machine, Duke the mascot, _Minecraft_, and “write once, run anywhere.” JavaScript clues: Brendan Eich, Netscape, making web pages interactive, and being written in about ten days. Never shorten JavaScript to “Java.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Java (prompt on “Java Virtual Machine” or “JVM”; do not accept “JavaScript”)

topics.name: Encryption
topics.kicker: Scrambling data with a secret key · Keeps messages and passwords safe
topics.dates: From ancient ciphers to RSA (1977) and AES (2001)
topics.briefing: Encryption scrambles a message with a secret key so that only someone with the right key can unscramble it. Julius Caesar shifted each letter three places down the alphabet, and in World War II, Germany trusted its Enigma machines, not knowing that Polish and British codebreakers had cracked them. Every time a web browser shows a padlock, encryption is protecting the data, often with math based on huge prime numbers.
topics.answerHtml: encryption (accept word forms like encrypting; prompt on cryptography, codes, or ciphers; do not accept “decryption”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Clifford Cocks invented a public-key method much like RSA at Britain’s GCHQ in 1973, but his work on this process stayed secret until 1997. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman’s 1976 paper showed how two strangers could agree on a shared secret key in public.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of scrambling a message so that only someone with the right key can read it.

tossups.p: In the ancient Spartan scytale [“SKIT-uh-lee”], a strip of leather was wound around a rod, and only a reader with a rod of the same thickness could read the message. Leon Battista Alberti’s cipher disk, from the 1400s, was another early tool for this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, reversed by decryption, that turns readable plaintext into secret ciphertext.

tossups.p: In 1998, the Electronic Frontier Foundation built a machine nicknamed “Deep Crack” that found a key for DES, a U.S. government standard for this process, by rapidly trying one possible key after another. DES used keys only 56 bits long.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of scrambling data so that it can be read only with the right key.

tossups.p: In 1586, Thomas Phelippes broke the cipher in letters between Mary, Queen of Scots, and the plotter Anthony Babington, and the plot they revealed led to Mary’s execution. Simple forms of this process that swap each letter for a symbol can be broken by counting how often each symbol appears.
tossups.r: It is reversed by decryption. For 10 points, name this process of turning plaintext into ciphertext with a key.

tossups.p: In the 800s, Al-Kindi, a scholar in Baghdad, described frequency analysis, which defeats simple forms of this process by counting how often each letter or symbol appears; in English, E is the most common letter.
tossups.r: Julius Caesar used a form of it that shifts letters three places. For 10 points, name this process of turning a message into secret code.

tossups.p: Friedrich Kasiski and Charles Babbage each broke a form of this process that uses a keyword to shift each letter by a different amount. That method is named for Blaise de Vigenère [“vee-zhuh-NAIR”], though Giovan Battista Bellaso described it first, in 1553.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, reversed by decryption, that scrambles messages so only someone with the key can read them.

tossups.p: At Bletchley Park, Tommy Flowers’s Colossus computers helped read top-level German army messages that had been scrambled with this process on Lorenz machines. Before that, Polish mathematicians including Marian Rejewski [“reh-YEF-skee”] had broken the Enigma machines that Germany also used for this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of scrambling messages with a secret key, which is reversed by decryption.

tossups.p: Claude Shannon proved that the one-time pad, which uses a truly random key as long as the message and never reuses it, gives perfect secrecy for this process. Shannon’s 1949 paper on “secrecy systems” helped turn this process into a science.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of scrambling information so that only someone with the right key can read it.

tossups.p: In the paper describing their RSA system, Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman called the sender and receiver “Alice” and “Bob,” names that became standard in this field. RSA’s safety depends on how hard it is to factor a product of two huge prime numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of scrambling data, which websites marked with a padlock use to protect passwords.

tossups.p: Phil Zimmermann released a program called PGP, short for “Pretty Good Privacy,” in 1991 so that ordinary people could use strong forms of this process on their email. The U.S. government investigated him after copies spread overseas but dropped the case in 1996.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that websites using HTTPS rely on to scramble data so only the right reader can unscramble it.

tossups.p: Peter Shor’s 1994 algorithm could let a large quantum computer break a common form of this process by quickly factoring huge numbers into primes. Researchers have designed “post-quantum” methods meant to resist such machines.
tossups.r: That form, RSA, uses a public key and a private key. For 10 points, name this process that scrambles messages with a key.

tossups.p: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman won the 2015 Turing Award for a 1976 method that lets two people agree on a secret key over a public line, a breakthrough for this process. Ralph Merkle had a related idea.
tossups.r: Their work led to public-key systems for this process. For 10 points, name this process, which is reversed by decryption.

tossups.p: Belgian researchers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen designed a cipher called Rijndael [“RAIN-dahl”], which the United States adopted in 2001 as AES, a national standard for this process. AES keys can be 128, 192, or 256 bits long.
tossups.r: It replaced an older standard called DES. For 10 points, name this process of turning plaintext into ciphertext.

tossups.p: In 2016, the messaging app WhatsApp finished turning on the “end-to-end” form of this process for all of its users, using the Signal Protocol, so that not even the company itself could read their chats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, also used by HTTPS websites marked with a padlock, that scrambles data with a key.

tossups.p: Unlike steganography, which hides the fact that a message even exists, this process hides what a message means. ROT13, a simple form of this process, shifts each letter 13 places, so doing it twice gives back the original text.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which Julius Caesar used when he shifted letters three places.

clues.t: Scrambles readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext so only someone with the right key can read it
Reversed by decryption, which turns ciphertext back into plaintext
The Caesar cipher shifts every letter three places, so A becomes D; ROT13 shifts letters 13 places
HTTPS websites, marked with a padlock, use it to protect passwords and payments
Symmetric methods use one shared secret key to lock and unlock a message
Public-key (asymmetric) methods lock a message with a public key and unlock it with a private key
RSA (1977), named for Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, is safe because factoring a product of two huge primes is so hard
The Vigenère cipher uses a keyword to shift each letter by a different amount
Frequency analysis breaks simple ciphers by counting how often each letter appears; Al-Kindi described it in the 800s
Germany’s Enigma machines did it in World War II; Polish codebreakers including Marian Rejewski, then Bletchley Park, broke them
A one-time pad, with a truly random key as long as the message and never reused, cannot be broken
AES, adopted by the United States in 2001, is based on Rijndael, by Belgians Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen
End-to-end versions, like the one WhatsApp turned on for everyone in 2016, keep even the app company from reading chats
Not the same as steganography, which hides the fact that a message exists at all
Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman’s 1976 method lets two people agree on a secret key in public; they won the 2015 Turing Award
At Britain’s GCHQ, Clifford Cocks found an RSA-like public-key method in 1973, but it stayed secret until 1997
The ancient Spartan scytale wrapped a leather strip around a rod; only a rod of the same thickness revealed the message
Leon Battista Alberti’s cipher disk, from the 1400s, was an early tool for it
Charles Babbage and Friedrich Kasiski each broke the Vigenère cipher in the 1800s; Giovan Battista Bellaso described it first, in 1553
Tommy Flowers’s Colossus computers at Bletchley Park helped read top-level German army messages scrambled on Lorenz machines
Thomas Phelippes broke the cipher in letters of the Babington Plot (1586), which led to the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
Phil Zimmermann’s PGP (“Pretty Good Privacy,” 1991) brought strong email protection to ordinary people
DES, a U.S. standard with 56-bit keys, was cracked in 1998 by the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s “Deep Crack” machine
Claude Shannon proved the one-time pad gives perfect secrecy; his 1949 paper on “secrecy systems” helped make the subject a science
The RSA paper named its sender and receiver “Alice” and “Bob,” names that became standard
Peter Shor’s 1994 algorithm could let a large quantum computer break RSA; “post-quantum” methods are designed to resist it

trap.title: Locking or unlocking?
trap.body: Encryption and decryption are opposite steps, and the two words differ by only a couple of letters, so listen carefully: a tossup about turning secret ciphertext back into a readable message wants “decryption.” Other answer lines sit nearby: cryptography is the whole science of secret codes, steganography hides the fact that a message exists at all, and hashing turns data into a fingerprint that can’t be turned back.
trap.fix: Encryption clues: plaintext becoming ciphertext, keys that lock data, the Caesar shift, RSA, AES, and the padlock in a web browser. If the clue is about reading someone else’s secret message, think decryption or codebreaking; if it is about invisible ink or a message hidden inside a picture, think steganography.
trap.line: Real answer line: encryption (accept word forms like encrypting; prompt on cryptography, codes, or ciphers; do not accept “decryption”)

topics.name: Central processing unit (CPU)
topics.kicker: The computer’s “brain” · Fetches, decodes and runs every instruction
topics.dates: First commercial single-chip version, the Intel 4004, 1971
topics.briefing: The central processing unit, or CPU, is the part of a computer that actually carries out a program’s instructions, which is why it is often called the computer’s “brain.” Billions of times every second, it fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, and executes it. The first commercial CPU on a single chip, the Intel 4004 of 1971, held about 2,300 transistors; by the 2020s, top chips held tens of billions.
topics.answerHtml: central processing unit (accept CPU, processor, or microprocessor; prompt on chip; do not accept “GPU” or “graphics processing unit”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stanley Mazor designed the first commercial single-chip version of this component, the Intel 4004, for a Japanese calculator company called Busicom. That 1971 chip held about 2,300 transistors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer component, often called the “brain” of the computer, that carries out a program’s instructions.

tossups.p: John Backus used the phrase “von Neumann bottleneck” for the way this component wastes time waiting while instructions and data travel back and forth between it and memory. In the von Neumann design, this component reads both instructions and data from the same memory.
tossups.r: This component contains an arithmetic logic unit and a control unit. For 10 points, name this part of a computer that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions.

tossups.p: The Spectre and Meltdown security flaws, revealed in 2018, took advantage of the way this component guesses ahead and runs instructions before it knows they are needed, a feature called speculative execution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer part, made by companies such as Intel and AMD, whose speed is measured in gigahertz.

tossups.p: In 1994, math professor Thomas Nicely found that Intel’s Pentium version of this component sometimes gave slightly wrong answers to division problems, a flaw called the FDIV bug. Intel ended up offering to replace the flawed chips.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of a computer, often called its “brain,” which runs the fetch–decode–execute cycle.

tossups.p: Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber designed a version of this component for Britain’s Acorn Computers in 1985, and that “ARM” design family went on to power nearly all smartphones. ARM originally stood for “Acorn RISC Machine.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer component, which contains an arithmetic logic unit and carries out a program’s instructions.

tossups.p: John Hennessy and David Patterson won the 2017 Turing Award for work that included pioneering RISC designs of this component, which use a small set of simple instructions. CISC designs, such as Intel’s x86 family, give this component many complex instructions instead.
tossups.r: Its arithmetic logic unit does the math. For 10 points, name this computer part, often called the computer’s “brain.”

tossups.p: Branch prediction helps this component guess which instructions will come next, keeping its pipeline full. Pipelining lets it work on several instructions at once, each at a different stage, much like cars moving down an assembly line.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this component, made by companies like Intel and AMD, that runs a computer’s programs.

tossups.p: Intel’s x86 family of this component is named for its 8086 chip of 1978. In 2020, Apple began moving its Mac computers away from Intel’s x86 chips to its own ARM-based M1 chip.
tossups.r: Its speed is measured in gigahertz. For 10 points, name this computer component that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions.

tossups.p: Unlike in the von Neumann design, the Harvard architecture lets this component fetch instructions and data at the same time from separate memories. Hyper-Threading, introduced in 2002, lets each core of this component handle two streams of instructions at once.
tossups.r: Its speed is measured in gigahertz. For 10 points, name this computer part, often called the computer’s “brain.”

tossups.p: In 1965, Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double every year, and in 1975 he changed his estimate to every two years. Chips for this component followed that “law” for decades.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer component, made by companies like Intel and AMD, that carries out a program’s instructions.

tossups.p: This component is made on thin, round silicon wafers by photolithography, which uses light to print tiny circuit patterns. By the 2020s, top chips of this kind held tens of billions of transistors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of a computer that carries out instructions in a fetch–decode–execute cycle.

tossups.p: A thin layer of thermal paste helps carry heat from this component into its heat sink. Gamers who “overclock” this component run it faster than its rated speed, so they often add bigger fans or liquid cooling.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer part, often called the computer’s “brain,” whose speed is measured in gigahertz.

tossups.p: Small, fast caches labeled L1, L2, and L3 sit inside or right next to this component so it doesn’t have to wait for slower RAM. Its registers are even faster, holding the few numbers it is working on at that moment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of a computer, often called its “brain,” that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions.

tossups.p: Chips with two, four, or more “cores” put several complete copies of this component’s working parts on one piece of silicon, so they can run several programs at the same time. A “64-bit” version of this component works with data in 64-bit chunks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this computer component, made by Intel and AMD, that carries out a program’s instructions.

tossups.p: This component’s program counter holds the memory address of the next instruction to run, while its accumulator and other registers hold the numbers being worked on. It only understands machine code, instructions written in binary.
tossups.r: Its arithmetic logic unit does math, and its control unit directs everything else. For 10 points, name this computer part.

clues.t: Often called the “brain” of the computer; it carries out the instructions of every program
Repeats the fetch–decode–execute cycle: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, then carry it out
Its speed is measured in hertz, usually gigahertz (billions of clock cycles per second)
Made by companies such as Intel and AMD
Its arithmetic logic unit (ALU) does math and comparisons
Its control unit directs the flow of data and tells the other parts what to do
Registers are tiny, super-fast storage spots inside it; the program counter holds the address of the next instruction
Caches labeled L1, L2, and L3 keep data close by so it doesn’t wait on slower RAM
Multi-core chips hold several cores that work at the same time; a 64-bit version handles data in 64-bit chunks
Built from billions of tiny transistor switches, printed onto silicon wafers by photolithography
Moore’s law: Gordon Moore predicted in 1965 that transistors per chip would double every year, then said every two years in 1975
A heat sink, fan, and thermal paste carry away its heat; overclocking runs it faster than its rated speed
It only understands machine code, instructions written in binary
In the von Neumann design, it reads instructions and data from the same memory
The Intel 4004 (1971), with about 2,300 transistors and built for Busicom’s calculators, was the first commercial single-chip version
Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stanley Mazor designed the Intel 4004
John Backus called the slow link between it and memory the “von Neumann bottleneck”
Spectre and Meltdown (2018) were security flaws in its speculative execution
The Pentium FDIV bug (1994), found by Thomas Nicely, made some division answers slightly wrong
ARM (first “Acorn RISC Machine”), designed by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber in 1985, came to power nearly all smartphones
RISC designs use a small set of simple instructions; CISC designs like Intel’s x86 use many complex ones
John Hennessy and David Patterson won the 2017 Turing Award for work that included pioneering RISC designs
The x86 family is named for Intel’s 8086 chip (1978)
Apple’s ARM-based M1 chip (2020) began replacing Intel chips in Mac computers
Pipelining overlaps the stages of several instructions, like an assembly line; branch prediction guesses what comes next
The Harvard architecture uses separate memories for instructions and data
Hyper-Threading (2002) lets one core run two streams of instructions at once

trap.title: CPU, GPU, or RAM?
trap.body: Several computer parts get confused with the CPU. RAM is short-term memory that holds data while programs run, a hard drive or SSD stores files for the long term, and the GPU (graphics processing unit) has thousands of small cores built for drawing images. The arithmetic logic unit and control unit are only parts inside the CPU, so naming one of them is too narrow.
trap.fix: If the clues mention fetching, decoding, and executing instructions, clock speed in gigahertz, or the Intel 4004, answer “central processing unit,” “CPU,” or “processor.” Clues about storing data mean memory or storage; clues about drawing graphics or graphics cards mean the GPU.
trap.line: Real answer line: central processing unit (accept CPU, processor, or microprocessor; prompt on chip; do not accept “GPU” or “graphics processing unit”)

topics.name: Linux
topics.kicker: Free, open-source operating system · Started by Linus Torvalds in 1991
topics.briefing: In 1991, a 21-year-old Finnish student named Linus Torvalds announced that he was building a free operating system, “just a hobby, won’t be big and professional.” That hobby became Linux, whose open-source code anyone can study, change, and share. Linux, whose mascot is a penguin named Tux, went on to run a huge share of the world’s web servers, all 500 of the fastest supercomputers by 2017, and, at its core, every Android phone.
topics.answerHtml: Linux (accept GNU/Linux or the Linux kernel; do not accept “Unix”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This operating system’s creator wanted to call it “Freax,” combining “free,” “freak,” and the letter x, but Ari Lemmke gave its folder a different name on a university’s file server. Version 0.01 of its kernel came out in September 1991.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this free, open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is a penguin.

tossups.p: Andrew Tanenbaum, the creator of the teaching system MINIX, started a famous 1992 online argument by calling this operating system “obsolete” because of its “monolithic” kernel design. Tanenbaum preferred small “microkernels.”
tossups.r: This system’s mascot is a penguin named Tux. For 10 points, name this open-source operating system started by Linus Torvalds.

tossups.p: In 2005, this operating system’s creator wrote the version-control system Git to manage its code, after a dispute ended the project’s free use of a tool called BitKeeper. Thousands of programmers around the world have contributed changes to its kernel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds in 1991, whose mascot is Tux the penguin.

tossups.p: Larry Ewing drew this operating system’s mascot in 1996 using GIMP, a free image editor. In 2022, this system’s kernel began accepting code written in the language Rust, not just C and assembly.
tossups.r: That mascot is the penguin Tux. For 10 points, name this open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds.

tossups.p: Ian Murdock named Debian [“DEB-ee-un”], one of the oldest versions of this operating system, by combining his own first name with that of his girlfriend, Debra Lynn. Debian’s releases are code-named after characters from the _Toy Story_ movies.
tossups.r: Ubuntu is built on Debian. For 10 points, name this open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds.

tossups.p: In 2012, this operating system’s creator shared Finland’s Millennium Technology Prize with stem-cell researcher Shinya Yamanaka. Years earlier, he had written its first version for his own PC, which used an Intel 386 chip.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system that Linus Torvalds released as a student in 1991.

tossups.p: IBM bought Red Hat, a company that sells versions of this operating system to businesses, for about 34 billion dollars in 2019. Red Hat had started Fedora, a free version of this system, in 2003.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is Tux the penguin.

tossups.p: This operating system’s creator announced it on Usenet in August 1991, writing that it was “just a hobby, won’t be big and professional like gnu.” He posted that message to a newsgroup about MINIX, the system that had inspired him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this operating system written by Linus Torvalds, the basis of Android.

tossups.p: Richard Stallman has argued that this operating system should be called by a longer name, because much of it comes from the GNU Project he began in 1983. Stallman also founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985.
tossups.r: That longer name puts “GNU” in front of its usual name. For 10 points, name this open-source system created by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is Tux.

tossups.p: Valve’s Steam Deck handheld game console runs a version of this operating system called SteamOS, and Google’s ChromeOS for Chromebooks is also built on it. Raspberry Pi OS, made for the tiny Raspberry Pi computers, is another version of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this free operating system created by Linus Torvalds, whose kernel is also the core of Android.

tossups.p: Version 1.0 of this operating system’s kernel came out in 1994, about two and a half years after version 0.01. That kernel is released under version 2 of the GNU General Public License.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system started by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is the penguin Tux.

tossups.p: Like the system Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built at Bell Labs in 1969, this operating system lets users type commands such as ls and cd into a terminal. Its users often work in the Bash shell and type sudo to run a command as an administrator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source, Unix-like operating system created by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is the penguin Tux.

tossups.p: This operating system is written mostly in the C programming language, and its “monolithic” kernel runs device drivers and memory management together as one large program. Its kernel can load extra pieces of code called modules while it is running.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system that powers Android phones, created by Linus Torvalds.

tossups.p: The “L” in LAMP, a popular bundle of web-server software, stands for this operating system; the other letters stand for Apache, MySQL, and PHP. A huge share of the world’s web servers run this system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system started by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is a penguin.

tossups.p: NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter, which made the first powered flight on another planet in April 2021, ran this operating system. By November 2017, all 500 of the world’s fastest supercomputers ran it too.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this open-source operating system created by Linus Torvalds, whose mascot is the penguin Tux.

clues.t: Created by Finnish programmer Linus Torvalds, who released it as a student in 1991
Free and open-source: anyone may read, change, and share its code
Its mascot is Tux, a penguin
Android phones run on a modified version of its kernel, the core of the system
Comes in many versions called “distributions,” such as Ubuntu
Announced on Usenet in August 1991 as “just a hobby, won’t be big and professional like gnu”
Much of a full system comes from Richard Stallman’s GNU Project (1983), so Stallman has asked people to call it “GNU/” plus its name
Its kernel is released under version 2 of the GNU General Public License
Unix-like: it works like the Unix system that Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built at Bell Labs in 1969
Inspired by MINIX, Andrew Tanenbaum’s small teaching system
By November 2017, all 500 of the world’s fastest supercomputers ran it, and a huge share of web servers use it
ChromeOS, the Steam Deck’s SteamOS, and Raspberry Pi OS are all built on it
Written mostly in C; its “monolithic” kernel runs drivers and memory management as one big program and can load modules while running
Users type commands like ls, cd, and sudo into a terminal shell such as Bash
The “L” in the LAMP web-server bundle, along with Apache, MySQL, and PHP
Torvalds wanted to call it “Freax” (free + freak + x); Ari Lemmke named its folder on a university server instead
Version 0.01 came out in September 1991, and version 1.0 in 1994
Andrew Tanenbaum’s 1992 post calling it “obsolete” started a famous debate over monolithic kernels versus microkernels
Torvalds wrote the Git version-control system in 2005 to manage its code, after a dispute over a tool called BitKeeper
Larry Ewing drew Tux in 1996 using the free image editor GIMP
Ian Murdock named Debian (1993) for himself and Debra Lynn; its releases are code-named for _Toy Story_ characters
Ubuntu (2004), from Mark Shuttleworth’s company Canonical, is built on Debian; its name is a Southern African word about shared humanity
Torvalds shared Finland’s 2012 Millennium Technology Prize with stem-cell researcher Shinya Yamanaka
IBM bought Red Hat, which sells versions of it to businesses, for about $34 billion in 2019; Red Hat started Fedora in 2003
In 2022, its kernel began accepting code written in the Rust language, not just C
Torvalds first wrote it for his own PC, which had an Intel 386 chip
NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter, which made the first powered flight on another planet (Mars, 2021), ran it

trap.title: Linux or Unix?
trap.body: Linux is “Unix-like,” but it is not Unix, which Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built at Bell Labs in 1969. MINIX is Andrew Tanenbaum’s teaching system that inspired Linus Torvalds, and GNU is Richard Stallman’s project that supplies many of the tools in a full Linux system. And don’t answer “Linus”: that is the creator, not the system.
trap.fix: Linux clues: Linus Torvalds, 1991, Finland, Tux the penguin, open source, Android, and distributions like Ubuntu and Debian. Unix clues: Bell Labs, 1969, Ken Thompson, and Dennis Ritchie. Saying “GNU/Linux” is fine, but “GNU” alone is a different answer line.
trap.line: Real answer line: Linux (accept GNU/Linux or the Linux kernel; do not accept “Unix”)

topics.name: Binary numbers
topics.kicker: Numbers written with only 0s and 1s · How computers store everything
topics.briefing: Binary numbers use just two digits, 0 and 1, so each place stands for a power of 2 instead of a power of 10: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. In binary, 101 means 5 and 1010 means 10. Computers use binary because their tiny transistor switches have only two states, off and on, so every photo, song, and text message is stored as a long string of 0s and 1s.
topics.answerHtml: binary numbers (accept base 2 or base two; prompt on number system; do not accept “bits” or “decimal”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The 1974 Arecibo [“air-uh-SEE-boh”] message, beamed toward the star cluster M13, was a string of 1,679 digits in this number system. Since 1,679 is 23 times 73, both primes, the digits can be laid out in a grid 23 digits wide to form a picture.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system, used by computers, that has only the digits 0 and 1.

tossups.p: Frank Gray patented a way of ordering numbers in this system so that only one digit changes at each step. In two’s complement, the negative of a number in this system is found by flipping every digit and then adding one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system used by computers, in which 101 means five.

tossups.p: After the Jesuit missionary Joachim Bouvet [“boo-VAY”] sent him diagrams of the hexagrams of the Chinese _I Ching_, whose broken and solid lines match this number system’s patterns, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz described this system in a 1703 paper.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system, used by computers, that writes every number with 0s and 1s.

tossups.p: Konrad Zuse’s Z3, finished in 1941 and often called the first working programmable, fully automatic computer, did its arithmetic in this number system, while the American ENIAC instead used the decimal system.
tossups.r: Single digits in this system are called bits. For 10 points, name this system that writes numbers using only 0 and 1.

tossups.p: More than 2,000 years ago, the Indian scholar Pingala [“PING-uh-luh”] described the rhythms of Sanskrit poetry using patterns of short and long syllables that work much like this number system. Centuries later, Francis Bacon’s cipher wrote each letter as a group of five A’s and B’s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system in which 1, 10, and 11 stand for one, two, and three.

tossups.p: John Tukey made up a short word for a single digit of this number system, and Claude Shannon’s 1948 paper on information made that word famous. Shannon used that word as a unit for measuring information.
tossups.r: That word is “bit.” For 10 points, name this number system that uses only 0 and 1.

tossups.p: Ancient Egyptian scribes multiplied numbers by repeated doubling and adding, a method that relies on the same idea as this number system. In this system, each extra digit doubles how many values can be written, so eight digits can show 256 values.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system whose digits, called bits, are always 0 or 1.

tossups.p: In ASCII code, the capital letter A is stored as the number 65, which is written 1000001 in this system. The largest number that one byte can hold is 255, written as eight 1s in this system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this base used by computers, which uses only the digits 0 and 1.

tossups.p: Every hexadecimal digit stands for exactly four digits of this system, so programmers use hexadecimal as a shorthand for it. A whole number written in this system is even exactly when its last digit is 0.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system whose place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on.

tossups.p: Using each finger as one digit of this number system, a person can count to 31 on one hand and to 1,023 using both hands. To change a number into this system, divide it by 2 again and again and read the remainders backward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system in which each finger is either down for 0 or up for 1.

tossups.p: A classic math joke says, “There are 10 kinds of people in the world: those who understand this system and those who don’t.” In this system, multiplying a number by two simply adds a 0 to its end.
tossups.r: The joke works because 10 means two in this system. For 10 points, name this number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1.

tossups.p: George Boole’s 1854 book _An Investigation of the Laws of Thought_ described an algebra of logic with just two values, true and false, which computer circuits later carried out using this number system. Boole’s logic uses operations such as AND, OR, and NOT.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system, used inside computers, in which 1010 means ten.

tossups.p: John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built a computer at Iowa State College in the early 1940s that did its math in this number system rather than in decimal. A 1973 court decision about the ENIAC patent credited Atanasoff’s earlier work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system, used by modern computers, that has only two digits.

tossups.p: Claude Shannon’s 1937 master’s thesis showed that circuits of electrical relays could carry out George Boole’s logic of true and false, laying the groundwork for doing arithmetic in this number system with electricity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system, the language of computers, that uses only 0 and 1.

tossups.p: Each Braille cell has six dots that are either raised or flat, so it can make 64 different patterns, just as six digits of this number system can write 64 different values. Those 64 include the pattern with no raised dots at all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number system that computers use, whose only digits are 0 and 1.

clues.t: Number system that uses only two digits, 0 and 1
Each place value is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and so on
Computers use it because their transistor switches are either off or on
One of its digits is called a bit; 8 bits make a byte
Examples: 101 is 5, 1010 is 10, and 1111 is 15
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz described it in a 1703 paper and linked it to the hexagrams of the Chinese _I Ching_
George Boole’s algebra of logic (1854) uses just two values, true and false, with operations like AND, OR, and NOT
Hexadecimal (base 16) is a shorthand for it: each hex digit stands for exactly 4 of its digits
In ASCII, capital A is 65, written 1000001
The largest number one byte can hold is 255, written 11111111; eight digits give 256 values
Using fingers as digits, you can count to 31 on one hand and to 1,023 on two
Joke: “There are 10 kinds of people: those who understand it and those who don’t” (10 means two)
A number written in it is even exactly when its last digit is 0; multiplying by two adds a 0 to the end
To convert a number to it, divide by 2 again and again, then read the remainders backward
The Jesuit missionary Joachim Bouvet sent Leibniz the _I Ching_ hexagrams, whose broken and solid lines match its patterns
More than 2,000 years ago, the Indian scholar Pingala described the rhythms of Sanskrit poetry with short and long syllables in a similar way
Francis Bacon’s cipher wrote each letter as a group of five A’s and B’s
Konrad Zuse’s Z3 (1941), an early programmable computer, used it, while the American ENIAC used decimal
John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry’s computer at Iowa State (early 1940s) used it; a 1973 ENIAC patent ruling credited Atanasoff
Claude Shannon’s 1937 master’s thesis showed that relay circuits could carry out Boole’s logic
John Tukey coined the word “bit” for one of its digits; Claude Shannon’s 1948 paper made the word famous
Frank Gray patented an ordering of these numbers in which only one digit changes at each step (Gray code)
Two’s complement stores negative numbers: to negate a number, flip every digit, then add one
The 1974 Arecibo message to the star cluster M13 was 1,679 of its digits, forming a 23-by-73 picture
Ancient Egyptian multiplication, by repeated doubling and adding, relies on the same idea
A six-dot Braille cell makes 64 patterns, just as six of its digits can write 64 values

trap.title: Number system or digit?
trap.body: A bit is one binary digit and a byte is eight of them; both are their own answer lines, so a tossup about storage units may want “bit” or “byte” instead. Other near-misses: decimal (base 10) is the everyday system with ten digits, hexadecimal (base 16) is a shorthand for binary, and Boolean algebra is the true-or-false logic that binary circuits carry out. Phrases like “binary star” or “binary search” are different answer lines too.
trap.fix: If the clues ask for a number system with only 0 and 1, place values of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, or how computers store data, say “binary” or “base 2.” If they ask for a single 0-or-1 digit, say “bit”; if they ask for a group of eight, say “byte.”
trap.line: Real answer line: binary numbers (accept base 2 or base two; prompt on number system; do not accept “bits” or “decimal”)

topics.name: Programming languages
topics.kicker: Tools for writing computer instructions · From Fortran to Python and Scratch
topics.dates: Fortran, the first widely used one, appeared in 1957
topics.briefing: Programming languages let people write instructions for computers in words and symbols instead of long strings of 0s and 1s. In the 1950s, Grace Hopper built one of the first compilers and John Backus’s team at IBM created Fortran; since then, programmers have invented thousands more, from C and Java to Python, which is named after the comedy group Monty Python. Many kids start with Scratch, whose code is made of snap-together blocks.
topics.answerHtml: programming languages (accept programming language or computer languages; prompt on languages or code)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Konrad Zuse designed one of the earliest of these, Plankalkül [“PLAHN-kal-kool”], in the 1940s, but it was not run on a real computer until decades later. Zuse had built the Z3 computer in Germany during World War II.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, such as Python and Java, that people use to write instructions for computers.

tossups.p: Alan Kay, who won the 2003 Turing Award, led the Xerox PARC team that created Smalltalk, which helped make “object-oriented” design popular among these tools. Other styles of these include “functional” ones like Haskell and “logic” ones like Prolog.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, including Fortran, C, and Python, used to write software.

tossups.p: Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie wrote a famous 1978 book, nicknamed “K&R,” about one of these that Ritchie had created at Bell Labs in the early 1970s. Ken Thompson and Ritchie used that language to rewrite the Unix operating system.
tossups.r: That book also made “hello, world” the classic first program. For 10 points, name these tools, such as C, used to write software.

tossups.p: Bjarne Stroustrup first called one of these “C with Classes” before renaming it C++. Stroustrup did that work at Bell Labs. Niklaus Wirth named another one, released in 1970, after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these languages, including Java and Python, that programmers use to write code.

tossups.p: Operators of the Harvard Mark II taped a moth into their logbook in 1947 as the “first actual case of bug being found,” a story made famous by Grace Hopper, whose work led to one of these named COBOL.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these languages, such as Fortran and Python, used to write instructions for computers.

tossups.p: Ada Lovelace’s 1843 notes on Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine included what is often called the first computer program, and the U.S. Department of Defense later named one of these after her. Her program was meant to calculate Bernoulli numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these languages, such as Java, C, and Python, used to write software.

tossups.p: John McCarthy designed one of these in 1958, built around lists, that became a favorite for early artificial intelligence research. The rules of another one, ALGOL 60, were written in a notation named for John Backus and Peter Naur.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, including Python and Java, used to write computer programs.

tossups.p: Apple introduced one of these named Swift in 2014, and in 2019 Google said that another, Kotlin, was its preferred choice for writing Android apps. Kotlin was created by the company JetBrains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these languages, such as Python, Java, and C, that people use to give computers instructions.

tossups.p: Graydon Hoare began one of these named Rust as a side project before Mozilla backed it, and its version 1.0 arrived in 2015 with a focus on memory safety. Another one, Go, was designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these formal languages, such as Python and C, that programmers use to write software.

tossups.p: A general-purpose one of these is called “Turing complete” because, given enough memory, it can compute anything a Turing machine can. Alan Turing’s 1936 paper described that imaginary machine. Conway’s Game of Life, which is not one of these, also meets that test.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, such as Python and Java, used to write computer programs.

tossups.p: Brendan Eich wrote one of these in about ten days in 1995 for the Netscape web browser, and its name was chosen partly to ride the popularity of a different one from Sun Microsystems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these languages, such as JavaScript and Java, that programmers use to write code.

tossups.p: Seymour Papert, Wally Feurzeig, and Cynthia Solomon created one of these named Logo in 1967, which became known for a drawing “turtle” that children steer around a screen. Papert, who had worked with the psychologist Jean Piaget, wrote about it in his 1980 book _Mindstorms_.
tossups.r: Kids can also learn with Scratch, whose code is made of snap-together blocks. For 10 points, name these tools used to write computer programs.

tossups.p: Guido van Rossum [“GHEE-doh van ROSS-um”] named one of these after the British comedy show _Monty Python’s Flying Circus_ and released it in 1991. Code in that language uses indentation, not curly braces, to group lines together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, such as C and Java, that people use to write computer programs.

tossups.p: Bill Gates and Paul Allen’s first product, in 1975, was a version of one of these for the Altair 8800 computer. That language, BASIC, had been created at Dartmouth College in 1964 by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tools, such as Python and Java, used to write software.

tossups.p: John Backus, who won the 1977 Turing Award, led the IBM team that released one of these in 1957 whose name is short for “Formula Translation.” COBOL followed in 1959 for business use.
tossups.r: That language, Fortran, was the first of these to be widely used. For 10 points, name these tools, such as Python, used to write computer programs.

trap.title: Category, not one language
trap.body: This answer is the whole category, so naming one example, like Python or Java, is wrong when a tossup asks for “these.” HTML describes how web pages are built and is usually called a markup language, not a programming language, and “algorithms” or “software” are the instructions themselves, not the languages they are written in. Natural languages like English and Spanish are a different answer too.
trap.fix: Listen to the pronoun. “These languages” or “one of these” means the general answer, programming languages. “This language,” with clues about one creator and one name, wants that single language, such as Java, Python, or Fortran.
